feedback.reason: A successful revocation must change the rule used by the authorization enforcement point. Checking a current credential/session epoch makes each new authorization decision reject sessions issued under the prior epoch; a queued notification or client-side cleanup is only propagation work.
feedback.details: Treat revocation as an authorization-state transition, not just an HTTP request being accepted. The identity authority advances a credential or session epoch (or marks the credential revoked), and each server-side check compares the session’s recorded epoch/status with the current value. The endpoint may return success only once the checks that protect requests enforce that value. If propagation is still pending, report pending/unavailable and fail closed at the affected boundary. Short token lifetime and refresh-token revocation reduce future exposure, but neither invalidates an already-issued access token immediately.

messages.text: A 30-minute residual lifetime means an old session remains usable after the endpoint reports success; expiry alone does not meet immediate revocation semantics.
Blocking refresh prevents renewal but leaves already-issued access tokens usable until expiry.
The queue write does not show that authorization checks enforce the revocation; a gateway that has not consumed the event still accepts the old session.
A client can be offline or malicious and cannot revoke a bearer credential at the server-side authorization boundary.

options.text: Advance the credential epoch and require authorization checks to enforce it before returning success.
Stop issuing tokens and document the remaining 30-minute validity window for existing access tokens; let them expire naturally before treating all sessions as revoked.
Revoke refresh tokens and keep validating existing access tokens locally until they expire; force users to authenticate again only on their next refresh.
Write a revocation event to a queue, return success immediately, and allow gateways to keep accepting old sessions until they consume it.
Return success after asking the client to clear its local session, while the server continues validating previously issued tokens.

prompt: After an administrator revokes a credential, the revocation endpoint returns success. Some access tokens issued before the revocation may remain unexpired for 30 minutes. What must the identity service guarantee before it reports revocation as successful?

feedback.reason: Acceptance and completion are separate states. A stable operation identity and durable job record make the acknowledgement recoverable; the worker lease recovers execution, and a read-only job resource reports progress without creating another job.
feedback.details: The HTTP response should acknowledge only a durable job record, typically with an operation ID and Location for a status resource. Persist the client intent and job state before returning 202; use the same client idempotency identity to resolve a lost response to the same job, and reject reuse with different parameters. A worker lease lets another worker resume after a crash. The request ACK does not claim the rendition is complete. GET reads the recorded job state and never schedules work. A long unary request can time out while processing continues, while an in-memory queue loses acknowledged work on process death.

messages.text: The 20-minute operation exceeds the caller’s 200 ms budget; a timed-out request does not reveal whether the original work continues, and a fresh submission can duplicate it.
A crash between the early response and durable persistence loses work that the service already claimed to accept.
A process-local queue cannot recover an acknowledged job after that process disappears; polling cannot reconstruct missing durable intent.
Status reads may be retried, cached, or prefetched; making GET start work violates safe read semantics and can create duplicate execution.

options.text: Create a durable job ID at acceptance and expose status and result through that resource.
Hold the request open through all rendition work; if its 200 ms caller deadline expires, ask the caller to submit a new job with a fresh request identity.
Return 202 when a process-local worker receives the request, then persist job state after the worker starts; retry a lost response by submitting again.
Put the job only in a process-local queue and return its ID; if the worker process dies, recreate the job from the client’s next poll.
Return a job URL whose GET handler starts or restarts transcoding whenever the caller polls for status.

prompt: A video service accepts a transcoding request and returns within 200 ms. The worker may crash immediately after acceptance, and the job can run for 20 minutes. What HTTP resource contract lets the caller retry safely and lets the system recover the work?

feedback.reason: A feature flag controls exposure, while data compatibility controls whether old and new readers can operate during rollback. An additive, dual-readable shape preserves the old contract until the rollback window closes; destructive cleanup is a later, separately gated step.
feedback.details: Treat the feature decision and persisted-data migration as separate changes. For this week of mixed app versions, the new field must be optional or have an old-reader-safe default, and both versions must read records written by the other. If writers populate both representations, define which one is authoritative and how conflicts are resolved. Turning the flag off must not require reversing an incompatible data rewrite. Only after old readers have been retired and rollback is no longer required should a later migration remove the old representation.

messages.text: A flag rollback does not reverse an in-place data rewrite; old app versions can no longer read records changed to the incompatible shape.
A stale client flag cannot restore server-side compatibility for persisted records or guarantee that old readers see a safe representation.
The stated one-week coexistence means old clients remain active; requiring simultaneous deployment violates that constraint and leaves no safe rollback path.
Dual writes alone do not define which representation readers trust or whether a rollback preserves the old reader’s interpretation.

options.text: Expand readers and writers compatibly before rollout; keep the data change reversible through the coexistence window.
Rewrite persisted records into the new shape before enabling the flag, then rely on turning the feature flag off to restore the old behavior.
Ship the new write format and keep rollback solely in a client-side flag cache that may remain stale after the server turns the feature off.
Make the new field mandatory in one coordinated release and require all clients to upgrade before serving requests.
Write both old and new fields during rollout but leave reader precedence and rollback interpretation unspecified; remove either field when the first new client launches.

prompt: A feature rollout must be reversible within five minutes while old and new app versions coexist for a week. Old readers ignore unknown optional fields; new readers safely default the new field when it is absent. What data-evolution contract keeps rollback safe?

feedback.reason: Idempotency is scoped to one intent. The invariant spans all intents competing for one resource, so the authoritative write must atomically reject any time range that overlaps an existing reservation.
feedback.details: Two buyers with distinct idempotency keys are not duplicate requests. Each can pass an earlier availability read, so neither a request key nor a read-then-write flow serializes the resource-wide rule. Put the overlap check at the reservation owner’s commit boundary: one transaction succeeds, and the other receives a conflict (or an explicit pending result until the same atomic claim resolves). A database exclusion constraint or a serializable transaction can enforce the invariant; an in-process lock works only if it truly covers every writer, which the multi-instance API does not. Never send confirmation before the authoritative claim commits.

messages.text: Idempotency prevents replay of one intent; the two valid keys represent different intents, so it does not prevent their ranges from overlapping.
Both requests can observe the same free state before either writes. Without an atomic check-and-reserve, both unconditional inserts can succeed.
Separate API instances have separate mutexes, so concurrent requests routed to different instances do not share the exclusion rule.
A later cancellation cannot make the original double confirmation true; users may already have relied on both bookings.

options.text: Enforce non-overlap atomically at the booking authority, independent of each request’s idempotency key.
Deduplicate identical retries by key, but allow each distinct key to insert its own reservation after the availability read.
Read the available slots, confirm both requests saw the slot as free, then insert each booking without a conditional write or exclusion check.
Protect the booking check with an in-process mutex on each API instance, while allowing requests to reach different instances.
Confirm both bookings immediately and run a background conflict resolver that cancels one booking later.

prompt: Two buyers simultaneously request overlapping appointment ranges for the same resource. Each request has a different valid idempotency key, and both availability reads show the slot as free. What must the reservation API enforce so that at most one booking is confirmed?

feedback.reason: The source sequence is 8400 but the searchable projection is applied only through 8360. Returning freshness metadata and an explicit not-yet-indexed state makes that gap observable instead of claiming the source object does not exist.
feedback.details: Keep the source record authoritative. Publish the source checkpoint and the highest contiguous sequence applied by the index, together with the query’s as-of watermark or lag. When a record is newer than the index watermark, return a stale/not-yet-indexed outcome or a bounded-staleness response; reserve not-found for a source-authoritative absence. A received-but-not-applied event is not enough evidence that search includes the record. This contract lets clients retry or explain freshness without silently turning projection lag into data loss.

messages.text: The known source record is committed after the indexed watermark; a 404 without freshness state misreports lag as absence.
A full source scan on every miss is unbounded and still gives the caller no way to assess the projection’s freshness.
A gap between source and index progress indicates work not yet applied, not deletion of authoritative data.
Receiving an event is not the same as applying it; the client needs the indexed/applied watermark to measure actual search freshness.

options.text: Expose the indexed-through watermark and return fresh results only after the query reaches the requested source sequence.
Return the same permanent 404 whenever the current index has no row.
On every index miss, scan the full source store synchronously and omit the index watermark from the response.
Treat the index watermark as the source of truth and mark every record after it as deleted until indexing catches up.
Record the last source sequence received by the indexer, but do not report which sequence has actually been applied to searchable state.

prompt: A media record is committed at source sequence 8400, while search indexing has processed only through 8360. A search for the known record returns no hit. What read contract lets the client distinguish indexing delay from true source absence?

feedback.reason: The two workloads have different deadlines and costs. Bounded weighted admission for batch work plus reserved urgent capacity prevents long recomputations from consuming every resource needed for the 100 ms path.
feedback.details: Estimate the resource cost of route recomputations and cap their concurrent and queued work. Preserve a lane or capacity budget for urgent dispatch, and return a clear deferred/rejected result for batch work when its budget is exhausted. A durable queue is useful for accepted batch jobs but does not itself provide latency isolation. Priority metadata also cannot preempt work already occupying all workers. Monitor queue age and urgent deadline misses so the reservation can be adjusted from observed load.

messages.text: A priority label alone does not reserve execution or admission capacity once long-running jobs occupy every worker.
Durability protects queued work from loss but an unbounded backlog can still delay urgent jobs beyond their 100 ms deadline.
Separate worker counts do not isolate the shared bottleneck; batch load can still consume the CPU or dependency urgent routing needs.
Retrying a saturated urgent request adds more work to the constrained path and worsens the deadline miss.

options.text: Reserve compute capacity for urgent routing so batch recomputation cannot consume its 100 ms budget.
Mark urgent requests as high priority but send urgent and batch work to the same unbounded worker pool.
Accept every batch recomputation into a durable but unbounded queue and let urgent work wait behind existing jobs.
Autoscale batch workers separately while both classes still compete for the same saturated CPU or downstream routing capacity.
Retry urgent route requests whenever they miss 100 ms, without limiting the number of callers or attempts.

prompt: A dispatch service must produce an urgent route within 100 ms. Nonurgent route recomputation can consume several CPU-minutes and may wait for a later batch window. What admission contract prevents batch work from exhausting urgent capacity?

feedback.reason: A timeout leaves the provider outcome uncertain, not failed. Stable identity and parameter binding make retries refer to the same intended charge; reconciliation must resolve that intent before a new one is created.
feedback.details: Persist the payment intent before calling the provider and bind the key to immutable request parameters such as amount and currency. Reuse the same provider idempotency key when retrying or querying the result. If the response is lost, expose pending/unknown and reconcile against the provider before changing the state to succeeded or failed. Reject a retry that reuses the identity with different parameters. A new key after timeout is a new financial side effect, and a later refund is weaker than preventing the duplicate in the first place.

messages.text: The provider may already have accepted the first request; a fresh identifier represents another charge rather than a retry of the same intent.
Gateway deduplication cannot prevent a duplicate side effect if each provider request has a new identity.
A response timeout proves only that the result is unknown; reporting final failure invites a second payment while the first may have succeeded.
Post-hoc detection and refund do not prevent the customer from being charged twice or guarantee recovery of the funds.

options.text: Keep one durable payment intent and reconcile its provider outcome before issuing another charge.
Treat the timeout as a failed charge and submit a new provider request with a fresh charge identifier.
Reuse a client request key at the gateway but send a new provider idempotency key on every provider retry.
Mark the payment failed as soon as the response deadline expires and tell the customer to try again with a new intent.
Create a second charge immediately, then compare provider settlement records later and refund any duplicate.

prompt: A payment provider times out after receiving an authorization request, so the merchant cannot tell whether it charged the customer. What retry contract avoids a second charge while the first outcome is unknown?

feedback.reason: The service has two explicit overload classes: accepted high-risk cases must persist, while low-value work may receive a visible defer/reject result. Durable admission before acknowledgment and bounded priority/fairness rules implement that contract.
feedback.details: Persist the high-risk case and its stable identity before returning accepted. Queue priority and reserved capacity keep low-value volume from consuming all admission slots, while fair scheduling prevents starvation among accepted cases. When the durable queue is full, return an explicit overload/defer response for low-value submissions and do not claim high-risk acceptance unless its record is durable. A priority bit alone is insufficient because it does not create storage or capacity. Track accepted-but-unprocessed age and rejected/deferred counts as overload signals.

messages.text: An in-memory or non-durable broker acknowledgment does not prove the high-risk case survives overload or process loss.
FIFO ordering lets a large low-value backlog occupy admission capacity and delay the high-risk cases the policy must protect.
A metric cannot repair the false acceptance response; an acknowledged case must have a durable record or the API must report defer/reject.
Scheduling priority affects work already admitted; it cannot recover a high-risk case that was never durably recorded.

options.text: Durably admit high-risk cases before acknowledgment and reserve review capacity for them.
Acknowledge high-risk cases when a broker accepts them in memory, then rely on consumers to rebuild any case lost during overload.
Put all risk classes into one FIFO queue and let the earliest low-value backlog consume the capacity needed by new high-risk cases.
Return accepted for every case, then discard low-value or high-risk records if the queue is full and count drops in a metric.
Give high-risk work the highest scheduling priority but acknowledge it before its queue record is durably stored.

prompt: A fraud service has limited review capacity. High-risk cases must never disappear after an acceptance response, while low-value cases may be deferred or rejected during overload. What queue admission policy meets both requirements?

feedback.reason: The export is a historical artifact. Its identity must pin both the source snapshot and the rules revision; a GET of that immutable identity returns the stored result even after later corrections.
feedback.details: Persist the export request’s period, source cutoff/snapshot identifier, rules revision, and completed artifact under a stable exportId. Once published, treat the bytes and metadata as immutable. A later payroll correction creates a new export identity; it does not rewrite the old export. This makes retries, audits, and downloads reproducible. A GET must only retrieve the artifact and must not silently rerun the calculation against current data.

messages.text: A period URL identifies the subject period but not the approved snapshot; recomputation can return different bytes after the correction.
Overwriting by period erases the originally approved output and makes an old retry silently refer to new data.
Updating inputs changes the meaning of an accepted exportId, so a retry may no longer reproduce the result first approved.
A cache keyed only by period can serve either old or new bytes without identifying which source cutoff and rules produced them.

options.text: Pin each download to an immutable export ID, source cutoff, and rules revision.
Use a stable URL such as /exports/2026-09 and regenerate its response from current payroll rows and rules on every GET.
Use the payroll period as the only export identity, overwriting the artifact whenever corrections arrive for that period.
Keep one export job row whose input snapshot and rules revision are updated to the latest values whenever a retry starts.
Cache the latest export response by period and rely on cache expiry to eventually replace it with corrected payroll data.

prompt: A payroll export for period 2026-09 is completed under tax-rules revision 17 and published as a downloadable file. Payroll data is later corrected under revision 18. Which resource contract makes a retry of the original export return the same approved output?

feedback.reason: A multi-table aggregate is meaningful only when its inputs share a declared consistency boundary. One snapshot/cutoff plus a returned watermark makes both the calculation and its freshness auditable.
feedback.details: Select a source snapshot or cutoff before reading accounts, invoices, and payments, then calculate every component against that same boundary. Include the period and as-of watermark in the output. If the storage system cannot provide a single snapshot, use a coordinated versioned cutoff and expose the weaker guarantee explicitly; per-table watermarks must not be presented as one coherent snapshot. Updates after the cutoff belong to a later report version.

messages.text: Combining independently current reads can include an invoice without its corresponding payment or balance update and produce totals that never existed together.
A wall-clock label does not make separate reads share a database snapshot; records committed during the run can still produce a mixed view.
Different watermarks explicitly show different source cuts, so the aggregate cannot be interpreted as one consistent report snapshot.
A later correction may be useful, but the original report needs a stable cutoff and a new version if its contents change.

options.text: Read every report aggregate from one consistent snapshot at the declared cutoff.
Read each table at its latest available state and combine the results, even when each read observes a different commit time.
Label the report with its start time but run ordinary reads over a period while new writes continue to appear.
Return a different watermark for each table and let consumers treat the combined totals as one period-end snapshot.
Publish the mixed-cutoff report as final, then expect a later background reconciliation to update totals without changing the report identity.

prompt: A financial report joins balances from accounts, invoices, and payments for a period ending at 2026-09-30. Updates can arrive while the report is running. What read contract keeps totals internally consistent and lets consumers know what data the report includes?

feedback.reason: The ingest burst and interactive query workload have separate capacity and latency needs. Bounded ingest admission plus an independent query budget prevents producers from consuming every query connection and makes overload visible.
feedback.details: Set a finite ingest queue or buffer, define whether excess telemetry is delayed or rejected, and communicate that state to producers. Give query serving a protected connection/worker budget so an ingest backlog cannot occupy it. Monitor ingest queue age, dropped/deferred events, and query latency. Durable buffering alone is not isolation if draining still shares the analyst query pool.

messages.text: An unbounded shared pool allows the 40,000-event burst to occupy connections needed to keep queries under 250 ms.
Priority applied after producers take every connection cannot protect the query path; capacity must be reserved at admission.
Silent loss contradicts an explicit overload contract and gives producers no signal to slow down or retry safely.
Durable buffering protects events from loss but a shared drain/query budget still lets ingestion consume interactive capacity.

options.text: Bound and isolate telemetry ingestion so analyst queries retain their own capacity.
Let producers and analyst queries share an unbounded connection pool and rely on database autoscaling to absorb bursts.
Keep one shared pool and prioritize query statements after ingest producers have already acquired all connections.
Discard telemetry whenever the database is busy, while returning success to producers and tracking only aggregate event counts.
Persist every burst into an unlimited buffer but give buffer draining and interactive queries the same workers and database connections.

prompt: A telemetry ingest burst reaches 40,000 events per second while analysts continue interactive queries against the same database. Query latency must stay under 250 ms; ingest may be backpressured with a visible overload signal. Which capacity contract isolates the two paths?

feedback.reason: A slow external provider must have its own bounded concurrency and queue plus a deadline that fits the caller budget. Bulkhead isolation contains its saturation so healthy providers keep their capacity.
feedback.details: Apply an outbound deadline shorter than the gateway’s 500 ms budget, reserve a finite number of in-flight calls for this provider, and bound any queue. When those limits are reached, fail or defer that provider’s request explicitly instead of borrowing every shared worker. A provider-specific circuit breaker can stop repeated calls during a known outage, but it should not trip healthy providers. Retrying is bounded and owned by one layer; it does not replace the deadline or concurrency cap.

messages.text: An 8-second wait exceeds the 500 ms budget and ties up shared workers needed by other providers.
An unbounded queue converts blocked threads into unbounded pending work and does not contain provider-specific resource use.
Immediate unlimited retries multiply load on the slow dependency and can keep all shared workers occupied.
A global breaker couples healthy providers to one dependency’s failure and turns a local slowdown into a broader outage.

options.text: Put the slow provider behind a bulkhead and enforce the caller deadline at the gateway.
Allow each request to wait for the provider’s full 8-second response in the common gateway worker pool.
Move calls to an asynchronous queue but allow its pending and in-flight work to grow without per-provider bounds.
Retry provider timeouts immediately in the same shared pool until a notification succeeds.
Use one circuit breaker shared by every provider, so repeated slowness at this provider blocks calls to healthy providers too.

prompt: A notification gateway calls an external provider that sometimes takes 8 seconds, while the gateway’s request deadline is 500 ms. Other providers share the same service. What dependency contract contains the slow provider’s impact?

feedback.reason: The append ACK must mean the attributed event is durable and tamper-evident. Access stays restricted, and after seven years removal follows an authorized audited purge rather than a silent edit.
feedback.details: Bind each record to the authenticated principal and a stable event identity, then persist it with integrity protection before returning success. Corrections are additional attributed events, not edits to the accepted record. Restrict read/write privileges. Preserve the record unchanged for seven years; after that, only the authorized audited purge process may remove it. A memory-buffer ACK does not prove durability, while indefinite retention and unrestricted deletion both violate the stated policy.

messages.text: A mutable row can erase the history of prior actions, so the ledger cannot prove what was originally recorded.
A process failure before the background flush can lose an entry that the API already acknowledged.
A client note is not trustworthy provenance; the authenticated principal must be bound by the append authority.
Immutability applies during the seven-year retention period; unrestricted access/deletion or retaining beyond the declared period without the audited purge violates the policy.

options.text: Persist an attributed, integrity-protected audit append before acknowledgment; permit purge only after seven years.
Store the latest audit action in a mutable row keyed by administrator and allow later updates to correct its text.
Acknowledge the append when a logger accepts it in memory, then flush records to durable storage in the background.
Write all actions under one shared service account and keep the original actor only in an optional client-supplied note.
Keep every immutable record forever and allow unrestricted administrators to read or delete any entry without a retention or purge audit.

prompt: A compliance service appends administrator actions to an audit ledger. Each record must identify its authenticated actor, be tamper-evident and immutable during a seven-year retention period, then be removed only through an authorized, audited purge. What append and retention contract meets this policy?

feedback.reason: Event identity handles redelivery of the same event; the monotonic shipment revision orders distinct events. The authoritative writer must compare the incoming revision with the stored one atomically so a delayed 41 cannot overwrite 42.
feedback.details: Persist the highest applied carrier revision alongside each shipment state. In one conditional transaction, accept a new event only if its revision is greater than the stored revision; treat the same event ID as a duplicate and quarantine or ignore a lower revision. If the carrier revision is absent, define another source-backed ordering rule before claiming monotonic state. Arrival time and broker order are transport observations, not substitutes for the business revision.

messages.text: Network arrival order can differ from carrier state order; revision 41 is older even though it arrived later.
A new event ID identifies a distinct event, but does not prove it is newer than the revision already stored.
Receiver timestamps describe delivery time, not the carrier’s sequence of shipment changes.
Broker ordering cannot establish source revision order across late retries or independent producers; the state owner must check the revision at commit.

options.text: Apply shipment state only when the incoming authoritative revision is newer.
Apply every authenticated carrier update in arrival order, assuming the most recently received message represents the newest shipment state.
Deduplicate repeated deliveries by event ID but accept any different event ID regardless of its shipment revision.
Use the receiver’s wall-clock arrival timestamp to order carrier state and overwrite the stored status with the latest arrival.
Assume the message broker preserves ordering across all carrier producers and write each delivered update unconditionally.

prompt: The shipment service has applied carrier revision 42. A delayed event carrying revision 41 arrives afterward with a different event ID. What source-of-truth write rule prevents the shipment from moving backward?

feedback.reason: The client intent must keep one stable identity across queue delivery and worker replacement. The processing record and side-effect owner use that same identity so an unknown result is reconciled before another billable call.
feedback.details: Persist the intent key with a hash of its parameters and an accepted/pending/complete/failed state. Reusing the key with different parameters is a conflict. Pass that identity to the billable provider when it supports idempotency, and keep the effect owner’s durable record so a retry can query or reconcile the original result. Queue deduplication and worker leases reduce duplicate attempts, but only an identity carried to the side-effect boundary prevents a fresh job ID from becoming a second charge.

messages.text: A new job ID turns recovery of the same client intent into a second operation, so the provider may bill for the extraction twice.
Queue-level dedup does not protect the external billable effect when the provider receives a new identity on each retry.
If the process fails after charging but before recording the result, the retry sees no ledger entry and may charge again.
Worker restarts and lost responses are compatible with duplicate delivery; an exactly-once framework assumption does not bind the external side effect.

options.text: Persist one stable extraction intent before the billable provider call and reuse it for retries.
Assign a fresh job ID whenever the worker restarts and treat each job as a distinct extraction request.
Deduplicate messages in the queue but send a fresh provider request identity whenever delivery is repeated.
Charge the extraction provider first and write the operation record only after a successful response is received.
Assume the worker framework executes each accepted job exactly once and omit a durable side-effect ledger.

prompt: A document extraction client submits one billable extraction intent. The response is lost after the provider may have started work, and a worker later retries through a new job process. What operation record prevents a second billable side effect?

feedback.reason: The caller deadline and the allocation result are separate facts. A stable intent with explicit pending/confirmed/failed/unknown state lets retries query the original operation, while confirmation follows the authoritative seat claim.
feedback.details: Create one durable allocation intent and make repeated submissions with the same identity resolve to it. Return an addressable status resource. Pending means work is accepted but no seat confirmation has been established; confirmed follows the atomic inventory reservation; failed is final only when the owner knows no allocation occurred; unknown/reconciling remains explicit after an ambiguous timeout. GET is read-only. This prevents an expired client wait from being mistaken for an allocation failure or an accepted queue message from being mistaken for a ticket.

messages.text: A timeout only means the response was not observed; the seat may already be allocated, so final failure can cause a duplicate retry.
Accepted work is not a confirmed allocation; issuing a ticket before the authoritative seat claim can oversell the seat.
Status polling may be repeated or cached; letting GET reallocate creates side effects and can reserve a different seat on each poll.
An unknown outcome must remain visible until reconciliation determines the result; collapsing it into a final state misleads retry behavior.

options.text: Keep one allocation intent and report UNKNOWN until the inventory authority resolves its outcome.
Return failed whenever the caller deadline expires, even if the allocation authority may have committed the seat.
Treat durable queue acceptance as a confirmed ticket allocation and issue the ticket before the seat claim completes.
Make GET status retry the allocation operation so each poll can attempt to claim a seat again.
Expose only success or failure and map any uncertain provider response to whichever final state is easiest for the client.

prompt: A ticket allocation request times out while the allocation authority may already have reserved a seat. The caller must be able to distinguish work still in progress from a final failure or confirmed allocation and safely check the same request again. What result contract should the API expose?
